artists.biography: Longpigs were a British alternative rock band who rose to fame on the fringe of Britpop in the 1990s; comprising Crispin Hunt (vocals), Richard Hawley (guitar), Simon Stafford (bass guitar) and former Cabaret Voltaire member Dee Boyle (drums) who was replaced by Andy Cook (drums) on their second album. Hailing from Sheffield, the group had success with singles such as "She Said", "On and On", and their well-received debut album The Sun Is Often Out (1996).

Longpigs.biography: Longpigs were a British alternative rock band who rose to fame on the fringe of Britpop in the 1990s; comprising Crispin Hunt (vocals), Richard Hawley (guitar), Simon Stafford (bass guitar) and former Cabaret Voltaire member Dee Boyle (drums) who was replaced by Andy Cook (drums) on their second album. Hailing from Sheffield, the group had success with singles such as "She Said", "On and On", and their well-received debut album The Sun Is Often Out (1996).

perplexity.description:
The Sun Is Often Out is the debut album by Sheffield indie rock band Longpigs, released in April 1996. The album emerged during the height of Britpop, establishing the band as significant players in the 1990s alternative rock landscape. Featuring vocalist and guitarist Crispin Hunt alongside guitarist Richard Hawley, bassist Simon Stafford, and drummer Dee Boyle, the record showcased the group's polished approach to indie rock with strong melodic sensibilities.

The album achieved considerable critical acclaim upon release, being named one of 1996's 50 best albums by both Q and Melody Maker. This recognition was bolstered by the commercial success of several singles drawn from the record. "On and On" reached the UK Top 20 and received substantial radio airplay, while the re-released version of "She Said" also climbed to the Top 20, and "Lost Myself" peaked at number 22 on the UK Singles Chart. The album's commercial viability and critical endorsement positioned The Sun Is Often Out as a landmark release for the band, establishing them as one of the more successful acts operating at the periphery of the Britpop phenomenon.
